Name: sae_payload_features
Title: Sparse Features of the Hidden Channel: SAE Latents Active During Teacher Generation Predict and Mediate Subliminal Transmission
Short Hypothesis: The subliminal payload corresponds to a small set of sparse, interpretable features in the teacher's activations that are active while it generates the ostensibly neutral data (numbers/code), and these same features are causally responsible for the trait shift in the student. We hypothesize that (i) a sparse autoencoder trained on the teacher can identify a compact feature set whose activation on generated tokens predicts which sequences transmit, and (ii) clamping those features during generation (up or down) monotonically increases or removes the trait acquired by the student, establishing a causal, feature-level description of the channel.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) show the signal is undetectable to humans and LLM judges and is not in the semantics, but do not attempt feature-level interpretability of the generation process. Sparse autoencoders (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023) decompose activations into interpretable features and support causal interventions, but have been applied to a model's own behavior, not to a covert data-transmission channel. Emergent-misalignment interpretability has found trait-linked directions but not in the subliminal-generation setting. We uniquely use SAEs on the teacher-at-generation-time to locate the payload's source and test its causal sufficiency for transmission.
Abstract: Subliminal learning hides a behavioral trait in data that looks trait-free, defeating semantic inspection. We hypothesize the payload has a sparse, interpretable footprint in the teacher's internal activations at generation time. Using a sparse autoencoder trained on the teacher, we decompose activations produced while the teacher emits neutral sequences (e.g., number lists) and search for features whose activity (a) is elevated relative to a non-trait teacher and (b) predicts, per sequence, the amount of trait the sequence transmits to a student. We then test causality: we generate data while clamping candidate features and finetune students, predicting that suppressing the features removes the trait while amplifying them strengthens it, in a dose-dependent way, without changing the surface form of the data enough to be caught by content filters. We contrast trait-linked features against random and high-variance control features, and check specificity by verifying that clamping unrelated features leaves transmission intact. Success yields a mechanistic, human-readable description of what the teacher 'writes into' otherwise neutral outputs and a principled generation-side control for stopping unwanted trait leakage during distillation. It also tests whether the subliminal channel is low-dimensional and feature-structured, or diffuse and unsummarizable, adjudicating between competing accounts of how the hidden signal is produced.
Experiments: Train or reuse an SAE on the teacher's residual stream at several layers.

Generate neutral data (numbers) from a trait teacher and a matched non-trait teacher; for each generated token record SAE feature activations; rank features by differential activation and by correlation with per-sequence transmissibility (measured via students finetuned on each sequence subset).
Causal generation intervention: re-generate data while clamping top candidate features to high/low values; finetune students; measure trait strength as a function of clamp magnitude (dose-response).
Specificity controls: clamp matched random/high-variance features; expect no change in transmission.
Detectability check: confirm clamped-generation data still passes an LLM-judge content filter, i.e., the manipulation is not making the trait explicit.
Cross-trait test: verify each trait maps to distinct feature sets, and that swapping feature sets swaps the transmitted trait.
Report predictive AUC of feature activity for transmissibility and dose-response slope for the causal intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: SAE features may be an incomplete or superimposed basis; the payload could be distributed across many small features not captured as a compact set.
Clamping features can degrade generation quality, confounding transmission changes with fluency changes.
Requires a trained SAE for the specific teacher, limiting the study to models where SAEs exist or can be trained.
Correlational feature selection risks false positives; causal validation is essential and may be weak.
Findings may be layer- and width-specific and not generalize across architectures.
